                 Recent advances in photorealistic avatar generation have enabled highly re-
                       alistic talking-head avatars, raising security concerns regarding identity im-
                  personation in AI-mediated communication. To advance in this challeng-
                   ing problem, the task of avatar fingerprinting aims to determine whether[cs.CV]            two avatar videos are driven by the same human operator or not. How-
                     ever, current public databases in the literature are scarce and based solely
                on old-fashioned talking-head avatar generators, not representing realistic
                    scenarios for the current task of avatar fingerprinting.  To overcome this
                     situation, the present article introduces AVAPrintDB, a new publicly avail-
                   able multi-generator talking-head avatar database for avatar fingerprinting.
               AVAPrintDB is constructed from two audiovisual corpora and three state-
                     of-the-art avatar generators (GAGAvatar, LivePortrait, HunyuanPortrait),
                   representing different synthesis paradigms, and includes both self- and cross-
                  reenactments to simulate legitimate usage and impersonation scenarios.
                      Building on this database, we also define a standardized and reproducible
                benchmark for avatar fingerprinting, considering public state-of-the-art avatar
                    fingerprinting systems and exploring novel methods based on FoundationarXiv:2603.26934v1
                Models (DINOv2 and CLIP). Also, we conduct a comprehensive analysis un-
                  der generator and dataset shift. Our results show that, while identity-related
                 motion cues persist across synthetic avatars, current avatar fingerprinting sys-
                 tems remain highly sensitive to changes in the synthesis pipeline and source
                 domain. The AVAPrintDB, benchmark protocols, and avatar fingerprinting
                  systems are publicly available to facilitate reproducible research.

1. Introduction

   Recent progress in photorealistic avatar generation has enabled the syn-
thesis of highly realistic talking-head avatars from a single picture, signifi-
cantly advancing applications in telepresence [1], virtual reality [2], digital hu-
mans [3], and AI-mediated communication [4]. Large technology companies1
and startups2 are actively investing in avatar-based interfaces, with applica-
tions ranging from virtual assistants and customer service agents to remote
collaboration platforms and personalized digital identities [4]. Industry re-
ports3 estimate that the global market for digital humans and avatar-based
communication systems is expected to grow rapidly in the coming years,
driven by advances in generative AI and increasing adoption of immersive
communication technologies.
   At the same time, the widespread availability of realistic avatar genera-
tion tools introduces new security and privacy risks. Recent incidents have
demonstrated that synthetic media can be exploited for impersonation at-
tacks, social engineering, and identity fraud. For instance, DeepFake-based
scams4 have been used to impersonate executives in video calls and fraudu-
lently authorize financial transactions, leading to losses of millions of dollars
in real-world cases5. As avatar-based communication becomes more preva-
lent, these risks extend beyond static DeepFakes to interactive, real-time
impersonation scenarios, where an attacker can control a synthetic avatar
that visually appears to be a legitimate user.
   In such settings, traditional authentication methods based on appearance
(e.g., biometric face recognition [5, 6]) become unreliable, since the avatar’s
visual identity is fully synthetic and can be arbitrarily chosen or manipu-
lated. This shift fundamentally changes the authentication problem: instead

of verifying who the avatar looks like, the system must determine who is
controlling the avatar.  This task is known in the literature as avatar fin-
gerprinting  [7].  Formally, the goal of avatar fingerprinting is to determine
whether two avatar videos are driven by the same underlying human iden-
tity. Given two synthetic avatar videos V1 and V2, generated by potentially
different avatar synthesis pipelines, the system must determine whether the
underlying driver identities match. It is important to highlight that the task
of avatar fingerprinting differs from the task of DeepFakes detection [8, 9, 10],
where the main goal is to distinguish real from synthetic content. In avatar
fingerprint both samples are synthetic.
   Despite the considerable security implications for the society, avatar fin-
gerprinting is a recent and barely explored topic. Existing studies presented
in the literature [7, 11, 12], suffer from limited reproducibility and insuffi-
cient evaluation under realistic up-to-date conditions.  Neither [7] nor [11]
have publicly released their avatar fingerprinting system. Furthermore, cur-
rent datasets are restricted in scope, e.g., the popular NVFAIR dataset [7]
relies on old-fashioned reenactment techniques (FaceVid2Vid [13], TPS [14],
LIA [15]) and is only available upon request. As a result, it is difficult to
advance in this challenging task and really know whether current avatar fin-
gerprinting systems truly capture identity-dependent motion cues or instead
rely on artifacts specific to a given dataset or synthesis pipeline.
   This limitation is particularly critical in light of the rapid evolution of
avatar generation technologies. Modern generators span multiple paradigms
(e.g., warping-based models [16], 3D Gaussian splatting [17, 18], diffusion-
based approaches [19], etc.), each introducing different motion transfer char-
acteristics, temporal smoothing behaviors, and artifact profiles. In real-world
scenarios, a deployed avatar fingerprinting system is likely to encounter avatar
videos generated by unseen AI models and under diverse conditions. There-
fore, evaluating robustness across generators and datasets is essential to as-
sess the practical viability of avatar fingerprinting.
   This gap motivates the present article with the following contributions:

   • New Avatar Fingerprinting Database: We introduce AVAPrintDB6,
     a publicly available multi-generator photorealistic talking-head avatar
     database for avatar fingerprinting. AVAPrintDB is constructed from
     two audiovisual corpora (CREMA-D [20] and RAVDESS [21]) and three

state-of-the-art avatar generators (GAGAvatar [22], LivePortrait [23]
     and HunyuanPortrait [24]), representing up-to-date realistic avatar sce-
      narios. It includes both self- and cross-reenactments, simulating legit-
     imate usage and impersonation attacks.

   • Benchmark and Systematic Evaluation: We define a standard-
      ized and reproducible benchmark for avatar fingerprinting, including
      identity-disjoint splits, predefined verification trials, and evaluation
      protocols. In addition, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of public
      state-of-the-art avatar fingerprinting systems on our proposed bench-
     mark, evaluating their performance under avatar generator and dataset
       shift, and also analyzing fairness in terms of gender, ethnicity, and age.

   • Exploration of Foundation Models for Avatar Fingerprinting:
    To the best of our knowledge, we investigate for the first time the use of
    DINOv2 [25] and CLIP [26] as feature extractors for avatar fingerprint-
      ing. Combined with a temporal attention module, we analyze their
      ability to capture identity-related behavioral cues and compare their
     performance against state-of-the-art landmark-based approaches.

   The remainder of the article is organized as follows.  Sec. 2 provides a
revision of the state of the art. Sec. 3 describes the details of our proposed
AVAPrintDB. Sec. 4 describes the proposed benchmark, including the exper-
imental protocol and public avatar fingerprinting systems. The experimental
results are included in Sec. 5. Finally, Sec. 6 concludes with key takeaways.

2. Related Work

   Avatar fingerprinting addresses the problem of determining whether a
synthetic avatar video is driven by its legitimate user or not, focusing on iden-
tity cues preserved in facial motion dynamics rather than visual appearance
alone. The problem is also related to behavioral biometrics [27, 28], where
identity is inferred from human dynamic patterns such as gait, keystroke,
or facial motion. Unlike traditional face recognition, which relies heavily on
appearance cues, avatar fingerprinting must operate under conditions where
appearance is synthetically generated and therefore unreliable.
   This section provides a revision of the state of the art in avatar finger-
printing. Sec. 2.1 summarizes recent advances in photorealistic talking-head
avatar generation. Sec. 2.2 describes publicly available databases for avatar
fingerprinting. Sec. 2.3 reviews avatar fingerprinting approaches.

2.1. Photorealistic Talking-Head Avatar Generation
   Photorealistic talking-head avatar generation aims to animate a target
identity using the facial motion and head pose extracted from a driving sig-
nal, typically a video sequence. This task is also commonly referred to as por-
trait animation [29], motion transfer [30], or talking-head reenactment [31].
It is important to remark that this task differs from related problems such
as novel-view synthesis [32], full 3D head reconstruction [33], or audio-driven
animation [34], as the goal is to preserve the appearance of a reference iden-
tity while faithfully transferring motion dynamics from another source.
   Early approaches to facial reenactment relied on parametric face models
and 3D morphable models to retarget expressions and head pose, enabling
real-time portrait manipulation and reenactment [35, 36]. The emergence of
deep generative models enabled realistic reenactment from minimal input,
particularly through motion transfer methods that animate a single portrait
using learned keypoint dynamics [13, 37].  Subsequent advances in neural
rendering and implicit scene representations improved realism and view con-
sistency [38, 39], while recent diffusion-based video generation techniques
have further increased photorealism and temporal coherence [24, 40].
   These methods can be broadly categorized according to their underlying
representation and synthesis strategy as follow:

   • Neural rendering approaches, such as NeRF-based (Neural Radi-
     ance Field) models, represent the head as a continuous radiance field
      learned from images [38, 41]. While they achieve high visual fidelity
     and view consistency, they typically require multi-view data and are
     computationally expensive, which limits their applicability in real-time
      or one-shot scenarios.

   • Gaussian splatting methods provide a more efficient alternative by
      representing the head as a set of 3D Gaussian primitives [16, 42, 43].
     These approaches enable real-time rendering and controllable anima-
      tion through parametric face models, although they may exhibit minor
     geometric inconsistencies.

   • Image-based warping methods operate directly in the image do-
     main by transferring motion using learned keypoints or flow fields [37,
      44]. These methods are computationally efficient and well-suited for



                                 5

real-time applications. Recent works such as LivePortrait [23] demon-
      strate that large-scale training and improved architectures can yield
      high-quality and stable animations despite the lack of 3D modeling.

   • Diffusion-based methods represent the current state of the art in
      visual quality. By conditioning video diffusion models on identity and
     motion signals, they generate temporally coherent and highly realistic
      avatar videos [24]. These approaches offer strong generalization capa-
       bilities but typically incur higher computational costs.

   Across these paradigms, different design choices lead to variations in mo-
tion transfer fidelity, temporal consistency, and artifact characteristics. These
differences are particularly relevant for avatar fingerprinting, as they can in-
fluence how identity-related facial dynamics are preserved or distorted. Con-
sequently, evaluating avatar fingerprinting systems across multiple avatar
generation methods is essential to assess their robustness under realistic syn-
thesis variability, which is the purpose of the present article.

2.2. Avatar Fingerprinting Databases and Benchmarks
   To date, the number of public databases and benchmarks specifically de-
signed for avatar fingerprinting is very limited. The NVFAIR database intro-
duced by NVIDIA [7] is currently the largest collection of reenacted talking-
head videos, with more than 600,000 videos. NVFAIR comprises scripted
and free-form monologues from 46 captured subjects (real data) as well
as synthetic reenactments generated with three methods (FaceVid2Vid [13],
TPS [14], and LIA [15]), although they are considered old-fashioned nowa-
days in comparison to state-of-the-art avatar generators, as discussed in
Sec. 2.1.  In total NVFAIR covers 161 unique identities (by including ad-
ditional CREMA-D [20] and RAVDESS [21] speakers) with self- and cross-
reenactments.  Access to NVFAIR is restricted via a request form.  Also,
benchmarking is not possible as the proposed avatar fingerprinting system is
not publicly available.
   To the best of our knowledge, the only fully public avatar fingerprinting
database and benchmark so far is the GAGAvatar-Benchmark [12]. How-
ever, it only covers a single talking-head avatar generator (GAGAvatar [22]),
limiting diversity in appearance and motion dynamics.
   The proposed AVAPrintDB and benchmark is publicly available and cov-
ers multiple up-to-date photorealistic avatar generators (GAGAvatar [22],

LivePortrait [23] and HunyuanPortrait [24]) and varied source domains (e.g.,
generator and dataset shift), allowing to evaluate state-of-the-art avatar fin-
gerprinting systems in realistic scenarios.
    Finally, as already mentioned in Sec. 1, it is important to highlight that
the task of avatar fingerprinting differs from the task of DeepFakes detec-
tion [8, 9, 10], where the main goal is to distinguish real from synthetic
content. As a result, public databases in the topic of DeepFakes detection
cannot be used for avatar fingerprinting.

2.3. Avatar Fingerprinting Systems
   The task of avatar fingerprinting is formulated as a pairwise decision prob-
lem: given two avatar videos, the goal is to determine whether they are driven
by the same underlying identity or not.  This differs from authentication,
which evaluates a sample against a claimed identity (e.g., access control sce-
narios), and from identification, where a sample is matched against a gallery
of known identities. Avatar fingerprinting constitutes the most fundamental
setting, as it isolates the ability of a model to capture identity-dependent
behavioral signals without relying on predefined identity classes.
   Early works on avatar fingerprinting demonstrated that such behavioral
cues persist through avatar generation. In [7], identity was modeled through
facial landmark dynamics using temporal convolutional networks, showing
that user-specific motion patterns can be discriminative even in highly re-
alistic avatars (they achieved around 87% AUC in their best setting). Sim-
ilarly, [11, 12] proposed a graph-based approach that captures structured
relationships between facial landmarks over time, obtaining similar results in
their respective experiments (86.6% and 83% AUC respectively).
  A common characteristic of existing approaches is their reliance on landmark-
based representations, which provide invariance to appearance and mitigate
the influence of rendering artifacts. However, this design choice may also limit
the ability to capture fine-grained visual cues present in the pixel domain,
particularly those related to texture-dependent motion or subtle temporal
inconsistencies. For this reason, in the present work, we explore for the first
time the use of Foundation Models (DINOv2 [25] and CLIP [26]) for avatar
fingerprinting, which can encode richer spatio-temporal information without
explicit geometric modeling.

3. AVAPrintDB: Proposed Avatar Fingerprinting Database

   This section provides the details of our proposed AVAPrintDB. In partic-
ular, Sec. 3.1 describes the selection of the real databases (i.e., source data)
and post-processing stage whereas in Sec. 3.2 we describe the photorealis-
tic talking-head avatar generators considered.  Finally, Sec. 3.3 details the
generation pipeline to build both self-reenactments (legitimate usage) and
cross-reenactments (impersonation) pairs.

3.1. Real Databases: Source Videos
  We select two widely used video datasets in the literature as they consider
realistic scenarios for avatar fingerprinting: CREMA-D [20] and RAVDESS [21].
Our selection is guided by three main considerations.  First, both datasets
are distributed under permissive licenses that allow redistribution and deriva-
tive use, making them suitable for constructing and releasing a reproducible
benchmark. Second, they have been employed in prior work on avatar fin-
gerprinting and behavioral biometric analysis, including [7, 12, 45], which
facilitates continuity. Third, they include structured variations in emotional
expression and scripted utterances. These characteristics enable controlled
experimental protocols in which different subjects can be evaluated while
producing identical sentences and emotional expressions. Such control is es-
sential for avatar fingerprinting studies, as it allows identity-related motion
cues to be isolated from linguistic content, affective expression, and other
confounding factors. For example, the datasets make it possible to compare
avatars of different individuals speaking the same sentence with similar affect,
or the same individual rendered through different avatar pipelines, enabling
fine-grained evaluation of biometric consistency.
    Initially, we also considered the real videos from the NVFAIR dataset [7],
which includes additional videoconferencing recordings from 46 participants.
Unfortunately,  its licensing terms restrict redistribution and limit demo-
graphic analysis (e.g., ethnicity, age, and gender), so we could not included in
the proposed benchmark. Consequently, CREMA-D [20] and RAVDESS [21]
provide the best balance between legal permissibility, experimental control,
and comparability with prior avatar fingerprinting research.

3.1.1. CREMA-D Dataset
  CREMA-D [20] (Crowd-sourced Emotional Multimodal Actors Dataset)
is a large-scale audiovisual corpus designed to study emotional speech and


                                 8

multimodal expression.  It contains 7,438 video recordings of 91 actors (48
male, 43 female) between 20 and 74 years, representing a demographically
diverse group with respect to race and ethnicity. Actors were recorded under
controlled indoor conditions with frontal viewpoints, consistent lighting and
high-quality audio capture.
   Each participant delivers 12 semantically neutral sentences, which are
performed using multiple emotional expressions: anger, disgust, fear, hap-
piness, neutral, and sadness.  The recordings exhibit natural variation in
intensity and articulation while preserving consistent linguistic content. All
videos were recorded on 460 × 360 pixels at 30 FPS.

3.1.2. RAVDESS Dataset
  RAVDESS [21] (Ryerson Audio-Visual Database of Emotional Speech
and Song) is a high-quality audiovisual corpus designed for research on emo-
tional expression and multimodal speech.  It includes recordings from 24
professional actors (12 female, 12 male) speaking and singing with a range of
emotional expressions. In this article, we use the speech subset, which con-
tains 1,440 video recordings corresponding to two repetitions of 60 scripted
utterances produced by each actor.
   Recordings were captured under tightly controlled studio conditions, in-
cluding uniform lighting, frontal framing, neutral backgrounds, and high-
fidelity audio and video. Actors deliver semantically neutral sentences using
multiple emotional states (neutral, calm, happy, sad, angry, fearful, surprised,
and disgust) with two intensity levels for all emotions but neutral. All videos
are 1280 × 720 pixels and were recorded at 30FPS.

3.1.3. Post-Processing Stage
  We discard the four videos reported by the creators of CREMA-D [20] as
corrupted, following the recommendations in their official repository7. We
further filter the dataset to retain only the 85 identities that contain at least
72 valid samples each. This result in a subset of 6,120 videos, ensuring a
minimum number of samples per identity and reducing class imbalance. In
addition, where metadata are available, the selection is stratified to preserve
diversity in gender, age ranges, and ethnicity.

  RAVDESS provides gender information for the recorded actors; for eth-

3.2. Photorealistic Talking-Head Avatar Generators
  A key aspect of our proposed AVAPrintDB is the inclusion of multiple
state-of-the-art avatar generators, each relying on different modeling assump-
tions and motion transfer mechanisms: one from the Gaussian splatting fam-
ily (GAGAvatar [22]), one from the warping-based family (LivePortrait [23]),
and one from the diffusion-based family (HunyuanPortrait [24]). These three
generators are selected as they represent distinct synthesis paradigms and


                                10

therefore introduce different types of motion transfer artifacts that may in-
fluence the avatar fingerprinting task.  They are specifically selected due
to practical considerations of availability, efficiency, and quality. GAGA-
vatar [22] is a one-shot 3D Gaussian head avatar method that reconstructs
a controllable 3D head from a single image in a single forward pass.  It is
lightweight in GPU memory and offers real-time reenactment speeds thanks
to its efficient 3D Gaussian representation, making it easy to use for our
purposes. LivePortrait [23] provides a fast, efficient 2D animation solution
with minimal memory overhead, and the code/models are publicly avail-
able. LivePortrait’s ease of use and high speed, combined with qualitatively
good visual results, made it a practical choice for our comparisons. Finally,
HunyuanPortrait [24] considers a state-of-the-art diffusion model. Although
diffusion models are heavier, HunyuanPortrait is open-source and produces
great visual fidelity and temporal consistency. Its inclusion allows to evaluate
a high-quality diffusion approach against the faster lightweight methods.
   From a biometric behavioral perspective, the generation process can be in-
terpreted as a transformation that maps real facial motion into a synthetic do-
main. Ideally, this transformation should preserve identity-specific temporal
patterns while altering appearance. However, in practice, avatar generators
may introduce biases, artifacts, or normalization effects that partially sup-
press or modify these cues. As a result, models trained or evaluated on a sin-
gle generator may inadvertently learn generator-specific artifacts instead of
robust behavioral patterns. To address this limitation, our proposed bench-
mark incorporates multiple generators with diverse characteristics, enabling
systematic evaluation under intra- and cross-generator conditions. This de-
sign allows us to analyze whether avatar fingerprinting systems generalize
across synthesis pipelines or rely on artifacts tied to a specific generator.

3.3. AVAPrintDB Generation and Analysis
   Based on the the curated datasets described in Sec. 3.1 and the avatar
generators described in Sec. 3.2, we construct our proposed AVAPrintDB de-
signed to support controlled and reproducible evaluation of avatar finger-
printing systems. Each generated video is defined by a target identity (which
determines the avatar appearance) and a driving identity (which provides the
motion dynamics). This setup enables both self-reenactment (same target
and driver) and cross-reenactment (different target and driver), as shown in
Fig. 1, which are essential for evaluating avatar fingerprinting. Every target-
driver pair is rendered with the same three avatar generators, ensuring that

4. Proposed Avatar Fingerprinting Benchmark

   Beyond the proposed AVAPrintDB itself, we also define a standardized
experimental benchmark, including publicly available avatar fingerprinting
systems, identity-disjoint development and evaluation splits, predefined veri-
fication trial lists, and evaluation procedures. This design ensures that differ-
ent avatar fingerprinting systems can be compared under identical conditions,
facilitating reproducible research and fair benchmarking. This section is or-
ganized as follows:  the details of the proposed experimental protocol are
included in Sec. 4.1 whereas in Sec. 4.2 we describe the avatar fingerprinting
systems considered in the benchmark, including the exploration for the first
time of Foundation Models (DINOv2 [25] and CLIP [26]).

4.1. Experimental Protocol
   This section describes all the details regarding the experimental proto-
col of the proposed benchmark. Sec. 4.1.1 describes the procedure followed

4.1.2. Experimental Scenarios
   Using the above protocol, we define three main experimental scenarios:

   • Intra-dataset, intra-generator: the development and evaluation of the
      avatar fingerprinting systems are performed on avatar videos generated
     from the same source dataset and with the same avatar generator.
     These are the baseline results.

   • Intra-dataset, cross-generator: the development and evaluation of the
      avatar fingerprinting systems are performed on the same source dataset,
     but the avatar generator used for development differs from the one used
      at the final evaluation. This evaluates robustness to avatar synthesis-
     model shift while keeping the underlying source domain fixed.

   • Cross-dataset, intra-generator: the development and evaluation of the
      avatar fingerprinting systems are performed using the same avatar gen-
      erator, but the source dataset differs between development and the fi-
      nal evaluation. This setting measures generalization across acquisition
      conditions, subject populations, and dataset-specific biases.

   All these experimental scenarios allow us to disentangle three impor-
tant axes of variation in avatar fingerprinting: identity generalization (un-
seen subjects), generator generalization (unseen avatar synthesis pipelines),
and dataset generalization (unseen source domains). This benchmark pro-
vides a controlled framework for understanding whether avatar fingerprint-
ing systems learn robust identity-related motion cues or overfit to dataset-
or generator-specific artifacts.

4.1.3. Performance Metrics
   Similar to previous approaches in the literature [7, 11, 12], we assess
avatar fingerprinting performance using the Area Under the Receiver Oper-
ating Characteristic Curve (AUC-ROC). This metric measures the ability of
the system to separate target from non-target trials across all possible deci-
sion thresholds, and is particularly appropriate here because it is threshold-
independent and robust to moderate class imbalance in the number of gen-
uine and impostor pairs. Unless otherwise stated, all results in the article
are reported in terms of AUC (%).

4.2.1. Deep Learning Methods
   To advance in the topic of avatar fingerprinting under realistic synthe-
sis conditions, we require systems that are reproducible, fully specified, and
publicly accessible. Although recent studies have been presented in the lit-
erature [7, 11], none of them have released their implementations, training
pipelines, or pretrained weights, making it impossible to reproduce their re-
sults or conduct fair comparative evaluations.

up to −28.9 (CLIP) and −27.7 (Fusion). These results indicate that models
trained on CREMA-D learn representations that are partially tied to the
statistical properties of that dataset and do not transfer well to RAVDESS.
   In contrast, the opposite transfer direction (RAVDESS →CREMA-D)
shows a different behavior. In most configurations, performance improves rel-
ative to the intra-dataset baseline. For instance, the Graph system improves
by +7.4%, +8.9%, and +2.5% AUC points for GAGAvatar, LivePortrait,
and HunyuanPortrait, respectively. Although some minor degradations are

generalize well to CREMA-D.
   This asymmetric behavior can be explained by differences in dataset char-
acteristics. CREMA-D contains a larger number of identities and samples,
providing greater variability in facial motion, expression, and subject ap-
pearance. While this diversity is beneficial for learning rich representations,
it may also lead to systems capturing dataset-specific patterns that do not
generalize well. On the other hand, RAVDESS is smaller and more con-
trolled, with more consistent recording conditions and more exaggerated,
actor-driven expressions. Training on such data may encourage the systems
to focus on more stable and salient motion cues, which transfer more effec-
tively to the more diverse CREMA-D dataset.
   The impact of dataset shift is also modulated by the avatar generator.
LivePortrait consistently exhibits the largest degradation under CREMA-D
→RAVDESS transfer, suggesting that the learned representations are more
sensitive to dataset-specific motion characteristics in this setting.  In con-
trast, HunyuanPortrait appears more stable across datasets, with smaller
performance variations, which may be attributed to the stronger temporal
consistency and smoothing effects of diffusion-based generation. GAGAvatar
shows intermediate behavior, with moderate degradation and consistent im-
provements in the reverse transfer direction.
   Regarding the different avatar fingerprinting systems, the Graph system
shows relatively robust behavior, with moderate degradation in the chal-
lenging transfer direction (CREMA-D →RAVDESS) and consistent im-
provements in the reverse setting.  In contrast, the DINOv2 and CLIP
systems are more sensitive to dataset shifts, particularly when transferring
from CREMA-D to RAVDESS, likely due to their reliance on appearance-
dependent cues and dataset-specific visual statistics. The Fusion approach
consistently achieves the best performance in the matched setting, but still
inherits the sensitivity to domain shift, indicating that combining models
improves accuracy but does not fully solve the generalization problem.
   These experiments demonstrate that dataset-induced domain shift is a
critical challenge for avatar fingerprinting. The strong asymmetry observed
between transfer directions indicates that not all datasets contribute equally
to learning robust representations. In particular, training on more controlled
datasets such as RAVDESS may lead to better generalization, while training
on more diverse datasets such as CREMA-D may require additional regular-

6. Discussion and Conclusion

   This article introduces AVAPrintDB, a publicly available multi-generator
photorealistic talking-head avatar database and benchmark for the task of
avatar fingerprinting. Its main strength is that it enables, for the first time
in a fully reproducible way, controlled evaluation of avatar fingerprinting sys-
tems across multiple state-of-the-art synthesis pipelines and source datasets.
This makes it possible to study whether current avatar fingerprinting systems
truly capture identity-related behavioral cues or instead rely on generator-
or dataset-specific artifacts.
   The proposed benchmark and results achieved using two state-of-the-
art public avatar fingerprinting systems highlight two main findings. First,
avatar fingerprinting is feasible under controlled conditions, supporting the
hypothesis that identity-related motion cues can persist after avatar synthe-
sis. Second, current avatar fingerprinting systems remain sensitive to both
generator and dataset shift. These results indicate that present methods do
not yet learn fully robust and invariant behavioral representations.
   Overall, AVAPrintDB provides a reproducible and extensible benchmark
for studying avatar fingerprinting under diverse synthesis and data condi-
tions. We hope it facilitates the development of more robust and practically
useful avatar fingerprinting systems for authentication in avatar-mediated
communication.
